title: Time Dilation in Special Relativity
short_intro: Time dilation is the phenomenon where a clock moving relative to an observer is measured to tick slower than a clock at rest in the observer's own reference frame. It is a direct consequence of the constancy of the speed of light in all inertial frames.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Conceptual understanding of proper time versus dilated time, the Lorentz factor, and basic numerical applications involving moving clocks and high-speed particles like muons.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Rigorous derivation using Lorentz transformations, transverse Doppler effect, twin paradox analysis, and relativistic dynamics applications.

prerequisites: Postulates of Special Theory of Relativity

concept_notes.heading: Proper Time and Coordinate Time
bullets: Proper time (t_0) is the time interval measured by a clock that is at rest relative to the events being observed, occurring at the same spatial point in that frame.
Coordinate time (t) is the time interval measured by an observer in relative motion with respect to the clock.
The measured time interval in the moving frame is always greater than the proper time interval.

concept_notes.heading: The Lorentz Factor
bullets: The magnitude of time dilation is governed by the Lorentz factor gamma = (1 - v^2/c^2)^(-1/2).
As the relative velocity v approaches the speed of light c, the Lorentz factor approaches infinity.
For speeds much less than c (v << c), gamma approaches 1, and classical Newtonian mechanics is recovered.

concept_notes.heading: Experimental Verification: Muon Decay
bullets: Atmospheric muons produced by cosmic rays at high altitudes have a proper mean lifetime of about 2.2 microseconds.
Without time dilation, classical physics predicts they would decay before reaching Earth's surface.
Due to relativistic time dilation at high speeds (v approx 0.99c), their lifetime in the Earth frame is extended, allowing them to be detected at sea level.

concept_notes.heading: Symmetry and Reciprocity
bullets: Time dilation is reciprocal between two inertial frames: observer A sees B's clock running slow, and observer B sees A's clock running slow.
The apparent paradoxes (such as the Twin Paradox) are resolved by noting that the traveling twin must undergo acceleration and switch inertial frames, breaking the symmetry.

derivations.title: Derivation of Time Dilation using Light Clock
derivations.conditions: Observer at rest relative to the clock versus an observer moving with constant velocity v.
steps: Consider a light clock consisting of two parallel mirrors separated by a vertical distance L, with a photon bouncing between them.
In the rest frame of the clock, the time for a round trip is t_0 = 2L/c.
In a frame moving horizontally with velocity v, the photon travels a diagonal path of length 2s, where s = sqrt(L^2 + (v t / 2)^2).
Using the constancy of light speed, the total time t in the moving frame satisfies (ct/2)^2 = L^2 + (vt/2)^2.
Substitute L = c t_0 / 2 into the equation and solve for t.
derivations.result: t = t_0 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) = gamma t_0

derivations.title: Derivation using Lorentz Transformations
derivations.conditions: Two inertial frames S and S' with S' moving at velocity v along the x-axis.
steps: Write the inverse Lorentz time transformation: t = gamma (t' + v x' / c^2).
For a single clock kept at a fixed position in frame S', the spatial position does not change, so delta x' = 0.
The time interval measured in frame S is therefore delta t = gamma delta t'.
Identify delta t' as the proper time t_0 and delta t as the dilated time t.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Time Dilation vs Velocity Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of time ratio t/t_0 (or gamma) on the y-axis versus velocity ratio v/c (from 0 to 1) on the x-axis. The curve starts at (0,1) and shoots asymptotically upward to infinity as v/c approaches 1.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that time dilation effects are negligible at classical speeds (v/c < 0.1) but diverge rapidly as an object approaches the speed of light.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in MCQs to identify the correct qualitative curve or to calculate gamma at specific fractions of c (e.g., v = 0.6c or 0.8c).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Rossi-Hall Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic setup of particle detectors placed at different altitudes on a mountain to count the flux of cosmic-ray muons.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that the flux of muons measured at lower altitude is significantly higher than what would be predicted without relativistic time dilation, confirming the stretching of their lifetime.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually in PGT exams as experimental proof of special relativity.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Hafele-Keating Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A conceptual flow diagram showing atomic clocks flown eastward and westward around the Earth compared to a reference clock at the US Naval Observatory.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Combines special relativistic time dilation (due to velocity) and general relativistic time dilation (due to gravitational potential) to confirm predicted clock offsets.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in advanced PGT questions integrating special and general relativity.

solved_numericals.question: A space rocket moves with a velocity of 0.6c relative to the Earth. A clock on the rocket ticks every 1 second according to an astronaut on board. What is the time interval for one tick as measured by an observer on Earth?
solution_steps: Identify the given values: proper time t_0 = 1 s, velocity v = 0.6c.
Recall the time dilation formula: t = t_0 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2).
Calculate the velocity squared term: v^2/c^2 = (0.6c)^2 / c^2 = 0.36.
Calculate the dilated time: t = 1 / 0.8 = 1.25 s.

solved_numericals.question: At what fraction of the speed of light must a clock move so that its rate is slowed down by a factor of 2? (i.e., measured time interval is twice the proper time).
solution_steps: Set the condition: t / t_0 = gamma = 2.
Write the definition of the Lorentz factor: 1 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) = 2.
Rearrange to solve for v^2/c^2: v^2/c^2 = 1 - 0.25 = 0.75.
Take the square root: v/c = sqrt(3)/2.

solved_numericals.question: A particle has a proper lifetime of 2 x 10^{-8} s. If it travels through the laboratory at a speed of 0.8c, what distance does it travel in the laboratory frame before decaying?
solution_steps: Calculate the Lorentz factor for v = 0.8c: gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - (0.8)^2) = 1 / sqrt(1 - 0.64) = 1 / 0.6 = 5/3.
Calculate the dilated lifetime in the laboratory frame: t = gamma * t_0 = (5/3) * (2 x 10^{-8} s) = 10/3 x 10^{-8} s.
Calculate the distance traveled in the lab frame: d = v * t.
Substitute v = 0.8 * (3 x 10^8 m/s) = 2.4 x 10^8 m/s.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumption: Relative motion between inertial frames is uniform and rectilinear. Limitation: Does not account for accelerating reference frames without invoking general relativity or instantaneous inertial frames.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Time actually passes slower for the moving astronaut, so they age slower biologically because their internal chemical processes physically change.
common_misconceptions.correct: Time itself in that reference frame runs slower; all physical, biological, and chemical processes proceed at the standard rate when measured in their own proper time.
common_misconceptions.why: Time dilation is a property of spacetime geometry, not a mechanical disruption of clocks or biological systems.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Time dilation only applies to mechanical or light clocks.
common_misconceptions.correct: Time dilation applies equally to all physical processes, including radioactive decay, chemical reactions, and atomic transitions.
common_misconceptions.why: All phenomena in a given inertial frame share the same coordinate time framework.

quick_revision: Moving clocks run slow: t = gamma t_0 where gamma >= 1.
